title: Persistent Recursive Worlds Enable Autonomous Software Evolution
hook: Instead of keeping the agent alive across a long project, keep the project alive and let agents be disposable — enough to grow a 250k-line Rust C compiler for $44.
key_points: Most agentic coding systems chase continuity through persistent sessions, memory, or manager agents holding shared context.
Genesis flips it: the software project is the persistent object; individual agents are finite-lived and replaceable.
A project is a recursive 'world' — each local world is an accepted version plus a repo path; only accepted changes advance history.
Recursive delegation moves work across paths, so no single agent has to hold the whole codebase in context.
From an empty repo, Genesis (on DeepSeek V4 Flash) built a ~250k-line Rust C compiler over 120+ hours and 1,000+ agent episodes for US$44 in tokens.
The authors report it passed the full c-testsuite and most LLVM/Csmith tests, and separately ported 13 MESA modules to Rust with 1.55–6.87x median speedups.
content_html:
Long-running software projects outlive any individual coding agent. The usual fix is to make the agent durable — long sessions, memory stores, a manager agent holding shared context. Beichen Huang and colleagues (arXiv, August 2026) argue for the opposite arrangement: make the project durable and let agents be short-lived and disposable.

Their system, EvoX Genesis, represents a codebase as a persistent recursive world. Each local world is pinned to an accepted version and a repository path; finite-lived agents propose local changes, recursive delegation pushes work down into sub-paths, and only accepted consequences advance the version history.
extra_html:
The headline demonstration: starting from a repository with no compiler at all, Genesis used DeepSeek V4 Flash to build a Rust-based C compiler of roughly 250k tracked lines. The run spanned over 120 hours and more than 1,000 archived agent episodes, and the authors report it cost about US$44 in model tokens — with the result passing the complete c-testsuite plus most LLVM and Csmith tests.

Two further experiments probe the claim. In a separate compiler world built with GLM 5.2, development kept going through repeated agent replacement while retaining full test performance — the point being that no single agent was load-bearing. And Genesis reimplemented 13 MESA modules (100k+ lines of Fortran) as a ~90k-line Rust workspace, reporting median speedups of 1.55–6.87x across six numerical workloads.

These are the authors' own reported results on self-chosen tasks, not a shared benchmark, so treat the numbers as an existence proof rather than a comparison. The transferable idea is the architectural one: for long-horizon agentic work, durable, accepted, versioned state may be a better place to put continuity than an agent's context.

related.hook: Across 930,000+ agent-authored pull requests, half the friction of merging code traces to the repository, not the agent — and AI contributions concentrate that risk 2x more than human ones.

related.title: Agents That Learn on the Job Without Weight Updates
related.hook: An agent that cracks a hard request today starts from zero tomorrow. Distil each episode into a retrievable rule and a frozen model gets 2.6x better — no fine-tuning.

flashcards.prompt: What does Genesis make persistent instead of the agent?
flashcards.back_html: The software project itself. Each local "world" is an accepted version plus a repository path; finite-lived agents come and go, and only accepted changes advance the shared version history.

flashcards.prompt: Why does making the project (not the agent) persistent help on long-horizon software work?

choices.text: Projects outlive any one agent's context or session, so continuity lives in accepted state rather than in memory an agent must carry
It removes the need for tests, since accepted versions are correct by construction
It lets a single agent hold the entire codebase in its context window

flashcards.explanation_html: Complex systems develop over timescales longer than any coding agent's lifespan. Genesis stores continuity in the versioned project, so agents can be replaced without losing progress — the paper reports development continuing through repeated agent replacement with test performance retained.

flashcards.prompt: What does 'recursive delegation' do in Genesis?
flashcards.back_html: It moves work across repository paths — a world can spawn sub-worlds at deeper paths — so responsibility is scoped locally instead of one agent reasoning over the whole repo.
